title: What Are T Levels, and What Is Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing?
text: What Are T Levels, and What Is Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing? Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Overview T Levels are two year, Level 3 technical study programmes, equivalent to three A Levels, that follow GCSEs and sit alongside A Levels and Apprenticeships as one of three main post 16 routes. This page explains what a T Level is in general, and what the T Level Technical Qualification in Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing (Level 3) covers specifically the Mechanical Engineering pathway , which is the only pathway this study guide covers (see Qualification Structure for why). T Levels combine classroom theory with a minimum 315 hour industry placement. T Levels as a qualification type T Levels are developed in collaboration with employers and businesses so the content meets the needs of industry and prepares learners for work. The three post 16 options for young people are: A Levels Apprenticeships T Levels Alongside the Technical Qualification (TQ) itself, every T Level requires learners to complete an industry placement of 315 to 350 hours (45 to 50 days) . City & Guilds is responsible for developing and delivering the Technical Qualification, but the full T Level (awarded by the Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education, IfATE) also depends on completing the industry placement and any other requirements IfATE sets. What is the Technical Qualification (TQ)? The Technical Qualification is the main classroom based part of the T Level. The Outline Content behind it was produced by T Level panels of employers and professional bodies, based on the same standards used for Apprenticeships, and City & Guilds has since amplified that Outline Content into the full specification. The specification uses a consistent structure throughout: Criteria the subject or topic that needs to be delivered and assessed, often supported by a Range that lists exactly what must be covered (for example, under "Design processes" the Range lists which specific processes need to be taught). What do learners need to learn? context on the depth and breadth a topic needs to be taught to. Skills a mapping reference showing which core, maths, English and digital skills are embedded in that piece of content. Who is this qualification for, and what does it cover? This qualification is for 16 19 year old learners who want to work in the engineering industry. It is designed to deliver a high level of knowledge about the engineering industry alongside the occupational skills needed to enter it known as threshold competence . A learner who completes it is well placed to develop full occupational competence with further support and training once in employment. Topics covered include customer and client requirements, principles of design, design processes, and communication in design. After the shared common core, learners choose one standalone Occupational Specialism: Mechanical engineering Electrical and electronic engineering Control and instrumentation engineering Structural engineering Centres work with local employers, who contribute demonstrations, talks and (where possible) work placements. What could this qualification lead to? This Technical Qualification focuses on the knowledge and skills needed to work in the engineering industry, preparing learners to enter it through employment or an Apprenticeship. Completing the qualification also gives learners the opportunity to progress onto higher education courses and training. It particularly suits someone not yet employed in the industry, or looking to enter it after mainstream education giving broad knowledge and understanding across engineering, plus the occupational and core skills needed to enter the industry. The content is set by a representative panel of employers from across the sector, so it prescribes the minimum knowledge and skills genuinely required to enter the industry, and the specification itself is approved by IfATE. Key terms Threshold competence having the core knowledge and skills needed to enter the occupation and industry, and being well placed to develop full occupational competence with further support once in employment. Technical Qualification (TQ) the classroom taught, examined/assessed component of a T Level. Outline Content the employer panel defined content framework (based on Apprenticeship Standards) that City & Guilds turns into the full specification. Occupational Specialism the one standalone specialism (of four) a learner chooses to study alongside the common core. Industry placement the mandatory 315 350 hour (45 50 day) employer placement that runs alongside the Technical Qualification. title: Qualification Structure and Assessment
text: Qualification Structure and Assessment Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Overview → Structure This page summarises the qualification "at a glance" its official numbers, requirements and assessment methods plus how the Technical Qualification (TQ) is actually built from its two components. Qualification at a glance Area Detail T Level route Engineering and manufacturing T Level pathway Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing City & Guilds numbers 8730 (Core), 8714 (Occupational Specialism) Qualification Number 610/0516/2 Age group approved 16+ Entry requirements No formal entry requirements are set by City & Guilds, but learners are expected to have appropriate attainment at Level 2 before starting Assessment Core knowledge tests: externally assessed. Core Employer set project: externally assessed. Occupational Specialisms: externally moderated First registration September 2022 Technical qualification structure The TQ is made up of two mandatory components , both of which must be achieved to gain the full T Level Technical Qualification: 1. The common core component (300 Engineering common core) Level 3, 680 GLH, 1000 TQT. This gives learners a broad base of knowledge and skills that applies across the engineering industry and every Occupational Specialism linked to this T Level, while also developing the core skills they'll need on the job. 2. One standalone Occupational Specialism, chosen from: Component code Unit Occupational Specialism Level GLH TQT 8714 31 321 Mechanical engineering (covered by this guide) 3 680 1000 8714 32 322 Electrical and electronic engineering 3 680 1000 8714 33 323 Control and instrumentation engineering 3 680 1000 8714 34 324 Structural engineering 3 680 1000 Occupational Specialisms develop the knowledge, skills and behaviours needed to reach threshold competence in an occupation meaning a learner's attainment is of a standard to enter that occupation and industry, with the expectation they'll build up to full occupational competence over time with proper support and training. What the key terms mean Guided Learning Hours (GLH) the average number of hours of direct delivery a unit requires (contact with tutors/trainers, formal learning such as classes and tutorials, and time spent preparing for and completing assessment), rounded up to the nearest five hours. Total Qualification Time (TQT) the total time a learner is expected to spend achieving the qualification, including GLH plus independent preparation and study time. Criteria and Range criteria set out the subject/topic to be delivered and assessed; the accompanying Range spells out exactly what must be covered under that topic. title: Student Progression and Careers
text: Student Progression and Careers Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Overview This page covers who the qualification is for, what's required alongside the classroom based Technical Qualification, and where it can lead. Who this qualification is for This qualification is for 16 19 year old learners who want to work within the engineering industry. There are no formal entry requirements set by City & Guilds, but learners are expected to have appropriate attainment at Level 2 before starting. It's designed for someone not yet employed, or looking to enter the industry after mainstream education. The qualification gives learners breadth of knowledge and understanding across the engineering industry, alongside the occupational and core skills needed to enter it and is built to support fair access, letting learners manage and improve their own performance as they go. Industry placement and other T Level requirements The classroom based Technical Qualification is only one part of the full T Level. To achieve the complete T Level, learners must also meet every other requirement set by the Institute for Apprenticeships and Technical Education (IfATE), including: An industry placement of 315 350 hours (45 50 days) with an employer. Any other IfATE requirements, such as licence to practise qualifications where relevant. Centres and providers work with local employers throughout the course too, not just during the placement employers contribute demonstrations, talks on the industry, and (where possible) the work placements themselves. What the qualification covers Across the course, learners build understanding of the engineering industry and sector, covering topics such as: customer and client requirements principles of design design processes communication in design Alongside the shared common core, every learner studies one standalone Occupational Specialism. Nationally there are four choices (Mechanical engineering, Electrical and electronic engineering, Control and instrumentation engineering, Structural engineering) this study guide covers Mechanical engineering only , the pathway taught at UTC Leeds. Threshold competence The qualification is designed to deliver a high level of engineering industry knowledge plus the occupational skills needed to enter the industry known as threshold competence . A learner who completes it is well placed to build up to full occupational competence, with the right support and training once in a job. Where it can lead The qualification focuses on the knowledge and skills needed for working in engineering, preparing learners to enter the industry either through direct employment or as an apprentice. Completing it also gives learners the option to progress onto higher education courses and training instead. Key terms Threshold competence having the core engineering knowledge and skills needed to be ready to develop full occupational competence on the job, rather than being fully competent from day one. Industry placement the mandatory 315 350 hour (45 50 day) employer placement required alongside the Technical Qualification to complete the full T Level. Occupational Specialism the one standalone specialist pathway (of four nationally) a learner chooses to study for threshold competence in a specific engineering discipline. title: Grading and Results
text: Grading and Results Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Overview This page explains how the Technical Qualification's two components are graded, and how they combine into the overall T Level programme grade. How the components are graded Component Grading scale Core A\ E Occupational Specialism Pass, Merit, Distinction Core component grading The core component grade is calculated by aggregating points across all the core's assessment components. City & Guilds publishes grade descriptors for each grade band; broadly: An A grade shows comprehensive understanding of the full range of engineering principles, applied confidently to both routine and non routine contexts; clear, well justified, logically linked responses to complex briefs; meticulous selection of processes, tools, materials, methods and health & safety considerations; a range of communication strategies adapted to audience; and high accuracy with genuine, critical self evaluation. An E grade shows only limited understanding of some key principles in routine contexts; general, sometimes superficial links between knowledge and problems, with partial reasoning; little awareness of how decisions impact design, manufacture or maintenance; a narrow range of communication strategies not always suited to the audience, with technical inaccuracies; and only some evaluation of performance, without guidance on how to improve. Candidates must complete every component to be awarded the Technical Qualification. Anything City & Guilds determines doesn't meet the standard is recorded as Unclassified (U) . Occupational Specialism grading The Occupational Specialism grade is based on grade boundaries set for Pass and Distinction , using judgemental evidence against the specialism's grade descriptors, review of Guide/Grade Standard Exemplification Materials, and statistical evidence. Pass and Distinction grade descriptors are published in the learner and centre occupational assessment materials. To achieve the Occupational Specialism, a learner must be recognised at threshold competence (Pass) meaning they: are well placed to develop full occupational competence, with further support and development, once in employment; are as close to full occupational competence as can reasonably be expected from classroom based study (classroom, workshops, simulated working, and supervised working environments where appropriate); have achieved at least a Pass in the relevant Occupational Specialism component. If a learner doesn't meet the minimum standard for either the core component or the Occupational Specialism, they receive an Unclassified (U) grade for that component. Awarding the overall T Level grade To achieve the full T Level (not just the Technical Qualification), a learner must complete every element of the IfATE T Level framework: the Technical Qualification, the industry placement, and any other set requirements (such as a licence to practise qualification). The overall T Level Technical Qualification grade combines the core component grade and the Occupational Specialism grade: Core grade OS: Distinction OS: Merit OS: Pass A\ Distinction\ Distinction Distinction A Distinction Distinction Merit B Distinction Merit Merit C Distinction Merit Pass D Merit Merit Pass E Merit Pass Pass Key terms Unclassified (U) the result recorded when a learner doesn't meet the minimum standard for a component. Grade descriptor City & Guilds' published description of what a candidate must demonstrate to achieve a given grade band. Guide/Grade Standard Exemplification Materials reference materials used to help set and maintain consistent Occupational Specialism grade boundaries. title: Core Component Overview
text: Core Component Overview Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Core Component The engineering common core (component 300) is the shared foundation every student studies before choosing an occupational specialism. It's worth 680 Guided Learning Hours and is designed as an introduction to engineering and manufacturing that helps learners choose their specialist pathway, covering the theoretical knowledge and practices common across the whole sector. It's assessed through two externally set exams plus an Employer set project. The shared engineering common core that underpins the Mechanical Engineering specialism. Purpose The common core builds the knowledge base every engineering role draws on, whatever specialism a student later chooses: how the sector works, essential maths and science, materials, mechanical/electrical/mechatronic principles, control systems, quality, health and safety, business awareness, and the professional skills to plan and deliver a project. Learners are encouraged to approach it through questions like "what are the different sectors in engineering and manufacturing?", "what mathematics and science are involved?", and "how do I manage and present a project?". The 17 underpinning knowledge outcomes On completion of the common core, learners understand: 1. Working within the engineering and manufacturing sectors 2. Engineering and manufacturing past, present and future 3. Engineering representations 4. Essential mathematics for engineering and manufacturing 5. Essential science for engineering and manufacturing 6. Materials and their properties 7. Mechanical principles 8. Electrical and electronic principles 9. Mechatronics 10. Engineering and manufacturing control systems 11. Quality management 12. Health and safety principles and coverage 13. Business, commercial and financial awareness 14. Professional responsibilities, attitudes and behaviours 15. Stock and asset management 16. Continuous improvement 17. Project and programme management Topics 1 8 are covered on Engineering Core, Part 1; topics 9 17 on Engineering Core, Part 2. Completing the common core also gives learners the opportunity to develop their maths, English and digital skills see Competency Frameworks. How it's assessed Part What it covers Weighting Exam Paper 1 Maths, science, materials, mechanical/electrical principles, mechatronics (topics 4 9) 35% of core Exam Paper 2 Sector context, representations, control systems, quality, health & safety, business, professional behaviours, stock/asset management, continuous improvement, project management (topics 1 3, 10 17) 35% of core Employer set Project A synoptic, industry style project drawing on the whole core 30% of core The common core is graded overall A E (or Ungraded). After the core comes the Occupational Specialism for this guide, that's Mechanical Engineering. Key terms Common core the shared knowledge component (300) every student studies regardless of specialism, worth 680 GLH. GLH Guided Learning Hours. Underpinning knowledge outcome one of the 17 numbered topic areas the common core is organised into. Threshold competence the level of knowledge and skill needed to be ready to develop full occupational competence on the job. title: Engineering Core, Part 1
text: Engineering Core, Part 1 Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Core Component → Engineering Core, Part 1 This page covers the first eight of the common core's 17 underpinning knowledge outcomes: working in the sector, its history and future, engineering representations, essential maths and science, materials, mechanical principles, and electrical/electronic principles. These map to Core Exam Paper 2 (topic 1 3) and Core Exam Paper 1 (topics 4 8) see the scheme of assessment page for exactly how the two papers split the 17 topics. Subsection numbers mirror the specification. 1. Working within the engineering and manufacturing sectors 1.1 Key principles and methodologies in engineering and manufacturing design Covers the types of manufacturing process (wasting, forming, shaping, joining, finishing, casting, additive), fitness for purpose (functional and environmental requirements), user requirements (design briefs, specifications), approaches to design (linear, iterative, inclusive, user centred, design for manufacture/assembly, sustainable design and the 6Rs: reduce, refuse, rethink, repair, reuse, recycle), research/testing methodologies, and communicating design requirements to technical and non technical audiences. Students need to know how different manufacturing processes and requirements shape a design, the steps of linear versus iterative design and how testing feeds into reaching a suitable design, and how to interpret anthropometric (ergonomic) data. Lesson slides for this section: Design Principles and Manufacturing Approaches (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 1.2 The role of maintenance, repair and installation in engineering Covers types of maintenance activity (planned, reactive, preventative, condition based monitoring), the roles involved (machine operator, maintenance engineer, maintenance manager), operations (monitoring, repair, shutdown, servicing), the tools/equipment/measurement devices used, installation requirements, and how new technology and environmental pressures are changing maintenance practice. Students need to know the purpose of each maintenance approach and its pros/cons, who's responsible for what, why shutdown/servicing happens, an overview of the tools and equipment involved, the reasons for commissioning, and how good maintenance reduces environmental impact and supports safe waste disposal. Lesson slides for this section: Maintenance, Repair and Installation (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 1.3 Approaches to manufacturing, processing and control Covers the scale of manufacture (one off, batch, mass, continuous), manufacturing infrastructure (functional, product and matrix arrangements, cellular manufacture, production lines), levels of automation (manual, computer aided manufacture/CAM, fully automated, robotic), and control infrastructure (performance monitoring, quality assurance, quality control). Students need to know how scale of manufacture relates to automation level, examples of products made at different scales, the different manufacturing infrastructures and their trade offs, and the purpose and application of CAM systems/software. Lesson slides for this section: Design Principles and Manufacturing Approaches (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 2. Engineering and manufacturing past, present and future 2.1 Sectors of the engineering industry An overview of the main activities, products and services across engineering sectors: aerospace, rail, agriculture, automotive, chemical, structural, materials, logistics, defence, electrical/electronic, control, medical, manufacturing, marine, petrochemical, power generation (renewables, non renewables, nuclear), telecommunications, and water/waste management. 2.2 Significant technological advances in engineering from a historical perspective Covers how developments like new materials, electrical power and lighting, the internal combustion engine, electric motors, replaceable parts and mass production, television, radio, automated machines, computers and the internet have shaped engineering and wider social/economic development (transportation, healthcare, housing, employment, sustainability). 2.3 Areas of innovation and emerging trends in engineering Covers how emerging technologies and trends (AI, VR, AR, digitalisation, robotics, drones, autonomous systems, distributed energy, hybrid technologies, cyber physical systems, IoT, cloud computing, sustainability/circular economy) could influence manufacturing and social/economic development going forward. Lesson slides for this section: Engineering Past, Present and Future (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 3. Engineering representations 3.1 Drawings and information conveyed by drawings Covers drawing types (CAD models, freehand sketches, isometric, orthographic projection, exploded views, block diagrams, flowcharts, circuit diagrams, schematics) and the information they convey: scale, title blocks, views, line types, surface finish, manufacturing detail, standard features (threads, nuts, bolts, pins, counterbore, countersink) and their abbreviations (AF, CL, DIA, DWG, MTL, SQ, CHAM, CSK, HEX, R, THD, UCUT, PCD), and graphical symbols. Students need to know the purpose and audience of different drawing types, the use of CAD systems, and how to interpret and present information, symbols and conventions on engineering drawings to BSEN8888 and BS3939 standards. 3.2 Dimensions and tolerancing on engineering drawings Covers linear, diameter, radius and angular dimensions, tolerances, limits and fits, and geometric dimensioning and tolerancing (GDT) symbols (datum, parallelism, perpendicularity, concentricity, straightness). Students need to interpret dimensions and drawing symbols and calculate tolerances, limits and fits. Lesson slides for this section: Engineering Drawings, Dimensions and Tolerancing (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 4. Essential mathematics for engineering and manufacturing 4.1 Applied mathematical theory in engineering applications A broad toolkit students must apply to engineering problems: Standard arithmetic ordering, integers, decimals, standard form, fractions, percentages, ratios, applying BIDMAS (brackets, indices, division, multiplication, addition, subtraction). Algebra factorising/manipulating equations, solving simultaneous and quadratic equations, indices, logarithms (base 10 and natural, including growth/decay problems), sequences (arithmetic/geometric progression, power series), matrices (addition, subtraction, multiplication). Geometry calculating areas of 2D shapes and volumes of 3D shapes. Calculus interpreting graphs (straight line, trigonometric, exponential relationships), finding the equation of a straight line (y = mx + c), standard differentials/integrals, and using differentiation to find maximum/minimum values. Trigonometry Pythagoras' theorem and triangle measurement, circular measure (radians/degrees), trigonometric functions and graphs, sine/cosine rules, common trigonometric identities, vectors (addition, dot and cross product). Statistical analysis range, cumulative frequency, averages (mean, median, mode), standard deviation, and probability in engineering contexts. 4.2 Number systems used in engineering and manufacturing Covers decimal, binary and hexadecimal number systems: how to identify and convert between them, and where each is used in engineering and manufacturing. Lesson slides for this section: Essential Mathematics for Engineering (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 5. Essential science for engineering and manufacturing 5.1 Units of measurement used in engineering Covers SI units (metre, kilogram, second, newton, m³, m/s, m/s², N·m, Pascal, kg/m³, and multiples/submultiples from tera to pico) and imperial units (foot, inches, yard, ounce, gallon). Students need to know the difference between base and derived units, which units apply to which properties, and how to convert between SI/imperial units and between multiples/submultiples. 5.2 Vector and coordinate measuring systems Covers vector and scalar quantities (distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration) and polar versus Cartesian coordinates, including converting between them when angles are in degrees. 5.3 Scientific methods and approaches to scientific inquiry and research Covers the scientific method (observation, questioning, hypothesis, prediction/simulation, testing, conclusion, iteration) and how to analyse, evaluate, synthesise and apply research findings and test results, considering accuracy, reliability, precision and replication. 5.4 Measurement equipment, techniques and principles Covers measurement equipment (rules, callipers, micrometers, gauges, dial test indicators, coordinate measuring machines/CMM) and principles (precision, accuracy, uncertainty, resolution, calibration, tolerance) what each piece of equipment measures, how to use it, and its relative accuracy and limitations. Lesson slides for this section: Units, Measurement and Scientific Method (PowerPoint, 18 slides) 5.5 Chemical composition and behaviours Covers atomic structure (atom, nucleus, electron, proton, neutron, valence, ion, element, molecule), chemical structure (solutions, suspensions, solubility, compounds and mixtures), the periodic table, chemical behaviour in electricity (cells, cell/power capacity, internal resistance), electrolysis, and how metals/alloys react with acids and alkalis including applications like etching, surface finishing, bonding, and oils/lubricants. Lesson slides for this section: Materials: Chemistry, Properties and Structures (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 5.6 Forces and motion in engineering Covers types of motion (rotary, linear, reciprocating, oscillating), pressure, vector representation of forces, balanced/unbalanced forces, moments, torque, equilibrium and coplanar forces applying the theory and calculations to solve practical problems. Lesson slides for this section: Forces, Motion and Energy (PowerPoint, 18 slides) 5.7 Fluid dynamics in engineering Covers hydrostatic pressure and thrust, centre of pressure, viscosity, Bernoulli's principle, immersion, flow characteristics (laminar, turbulent, vortices, separation points) and aerodynamics (drag, thrust, lift) applying theory and calculations, and knowing the key differences between liquid flow and aerodynamics. 5.8 Thermodynamics in engineering Covers heat transfer mechanisms (conduction, convection, radiation), open/closed systems, sensible and latent heat, expansivity, and the gas laws (Boyle's law, Charles' law, the general and characteristic gas equations) applying theory and calculations to practical thermodynamics problems. Lesson slides for this section: Fluid Dynamics and Thermodynamics (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 6. Materials and their properties 6.1 Physical and mechanical properties of materials Physical properties: density, melting point, thermal/electrical conductivity, thermal expansivity, corrosion resistance, specific heat capacity, hardenability, weldability, permeability, permittivity, recyclability. Mechanical properties: strength (tensile, compressive, shear, torsion), hardness, toughness, brittleness, ductility, elasticity, plasticity, malleability. Students need to know the difference between physical and mechanical properties, define each, and calculate density. 6.2 Types of material and their structures Covers ferrous metals, non ferrous metals, thermoplastic and thermosetting polymers, elastomers, composites (GRP, CRP, MDF), engineering ceramics, timber, and smart materials (shape memory alloys, quantum tunnelling composites, thermochromic/photochromic materials, piezoelectric crystals), plus structural concepts: atomic structure, bonding mechanisms (metallic, covalent, ionic, van der Waals), microstructure, lattice structure, crosslinking of polymers, and composite structures. Lesson slides for this section: Materials: Chemistry, Properties and Structures (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 6.3 The effects of processing techniques on materials Covers how processing affects material structure and properties: forming (rolling, forging, press forming), welding, brazing, casting, sintering, coating, hot/cold working for metals; temperature and pressure for thermoplastics; curing for thermosets; sintering pressure/firing temperature for ceramics; and how reinforcement alignment/matrix ratio affects composite properties. 6.4 Heat treatments and surface treatments Heat treatments: case hardening, quench hardening, tempering, normalising, annealing, precipitation hardening. Surface treatments: painting, plastic coating, galvanising, electrolytic (galvanic) protection. Students need to know how each affects structure/properties and their common applications. 6.5 Causes of material failure and their prevention Causes: corrosion (oxidation, chemical attack, stress corrosion), ageing, and physical failure (deformation, fracture, fatigue, creep, erosion). Prevention: coatings, sacrificial anodes/cathodes, galvanising. Students need to know how corrosion causes material loss and perforation, the factors behind fatigue and the three stages of creep, and how different prevention methods compare. 6.6 Materials testing methods and interpretation of results Methods: visual inspection, tensile testing, toughness testing, hardness testing, corrosion resistance, wear resistance, fatigue (Wohler) testing, electrical conductivity. Interpretation: Hooke's law, load extension graphs (tensile strength, elastic limit, ultimate tensile strength, plastic deformation, stress/strain/Young's modulus calculations), characteristic graphs for different materials, and necking/transition zones in steel. Lesson slides for this section: Material Processing, Treatment, Failure and Testing (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 7. Mechanical principles 7.1 Principles of motion and mechanics in engineering and manufacturing systems Covers Newton's three laws of motion, types of forces (concurrent, non concurrent, co planar, non contact), and simply supported beams (loading types, load distribution, reaction forces, shear force, bending moments) applying Newton's laws with calculations and calculating beam variables. 7.2 Principles of forces and energy Covers conservation of momentum and energy, D'Alembert's principle, potential/kinetic energy, gravitational force, frictional resistance, mechanical work and power, and types of power source (mechanical, electrical, renewable). Students calculate displacement, velocity and acceleration for falling objects and collisions, explain tractive effort/braking force/friction/rotational kinetic energy/moment of inertia in practical contexts (flywheels, springs, pressurised fluids), and compare power sources (solar, hydro, wind, biofuel, geothermal, electric motors, internal combustion, fossil fuels, nuclear). Lesson slides for this section: Forces, Motion and Energy (PowerPoint, 18 slides) 8. Electrical and electronic principles 8.1 Principles of electrical and electronic systems A broad topic covering: basic electricity/electronics (flow of electrons, charge, energy, power, current, capacitance, waves, conduction, magnetism, electromagnetism, inductance, measurement of electrical quantities); electric circuit theory (voltage, AC/DC current, power, resistance, potential dividers, Ohm's law across series/parallel/combination circuits, Kirchhoff's laws, phasor diagrams, protection systems like lightning arrestors and RCDs); DC circuit networks (resistors/capacitors/inductors in series/parallel/combined circuits, semiconductors, hierarchical design); and signals (analogue vs. digital, waveform types, signal processing/conditioning, fan in/fan out). Students need to understand the physical principles behind electrical/electronic systems, magnetism and electromagnetism, circuit theory terminology and its use with Ohm's law to calculate voltage/current/resistance, AC voltage current power relationships (including graphs and phasor diagrams), protection scheme operation (differential and transformer protection), DC network characteristics including time constants, semiconductor diode/transistor properties and applications, and the characteristics of analogue versus digital signals and systems. Lesson slides for this section: Electrical and Electronic Principles (PowerPoint, 16 slides) Teaching resources Ready made lesson slides for this topic. Each PowerPoint includes learning objectives, a starter, teaching slides, a quiz with answers, an activity and an exit ticket, with teacher notes on every slide. Download it and adapt it for your class. Key terms Underpinning knowledge outcome one of the 17 numbered topic areas the engineering common core is organised into. BIDMAS the order of arithmetical operations: brackets, indices, division, multiplication, addition, subtraction. GDT geometric dimensioning and tolerancing, the symbol system for specifying allowable variation on engineering drawings. Anthropometric data measurements of human body dimensions, used in ergonomic design. Phasor diagram a graphical way of representing the phase relationship between AC voltage and current. title: Engineering Core, Part 2
text: Engineering Core, Part 2 Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Core Component → Engineering Core, Part 2 This page covers the remaining nine of the common core's 17 underpinning knowledge outcomes: mechatronics, control systems, quality management, health and safety, business/financial awareness, professional behaviours, stock and asset management, continuous improvement, and project management. Topic 9 (Mechatronics) maps to Core Exam Paper 1; topics 10 17 map to Core Exam Paper 2. Subsection numbers mirror the specification. 9. Mechatronics 9.1 The key components of a mechatronics system Mechatronics is the integration of mechanical and electronic systems into one functioning system. Mechanical components include gears, cams, linkages, levers and pulleys; electrical/electronic components include sensors, transducers, microprocessors, microcontrollers and actuators; common drive devices include standard electrical motors, servo motors and stepper motors. Students need to know the purpose and function of each component type. 9.2 The operation, function and applications of programmable logic controllers (PLC) in mechatronic systems Covers PLC types (unitary, unitary with modular features, modular) and architecture; operation (sensor signal conditioning, programming); function (process blocks, motor driver integrated circuits, interface devices); and applications (robotic arms, conveyor belts, packaging, SCADA, remote technical units, animatronics). Students need to know the differences between PLC types, how a PLC operates, and the advantages/limitations of PLCs versus alternatives like dedicated integrated circuits or computer based systems. 9.3 The basic principles of hydraulics and pneumatics Covers the transmission of power, fluid compressibility, and components (valves, pumps, actuators, cylinders, compressors). Students need to know the differences between hydraulic and pneumatic systems and their relative advantages/limitations, and how the components function and appear on schematic diagrams. Lesson slides for this section: Mechatronics, PLCs, Hydraulics and Pneumatics (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 10. Engineering and manufacturing control systems 10.1 Principles and applications of control system theory Covers inputs, processes (logic gates AND/OR/NOT, timers, comparators, pulse units, counters, latches), outputs, signals, feedback, open/closed loop systems, transfer functions, summing points, analogue/digital signals, pulse width/amplitude modulation, and how control systems are represented in diagrams applied to electrical, pneumatic and hydraulic systems measuring pressure, flow, temperature, speed or position. Students need to be able to produce and explain a system diagram with multiple inputs/outputs and feedback, know the applications and trade offs of open versus closed loop control (including under/over damping and time dependency), understand steady state error, compare analogue and digital signals, and know industry applications including networked communication and data transmission. 10.2 How sensors and actuators are used in automation control systems Covers sensor/actuator types (analogue, digital, active, passive), applications (switches, proximity sensors, laser, vision systems), power sources, and hard wired versus wireless connections; and their uses in automation (positioning/measuring objects, mechanised lifting and moving, and measurement across electrical, mechanical, thermal, chemical, biological, optical and acoustic/radiation domains). Lesson slides for this section: Control Systems, Sensors and Actuators (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 11. Quality management 11.1 Quality standards, assurance, control and improvement Standards: British standards, ISO standards, CE marking, and professional engineering bodies (Engineering Council, IET, IMechE, SOE, CIBSE, IAgrE, IMI, TWI). Assurance and control: a culture of quality, "right first time," ISO 9001, inspection/testing, traceability, document/version control, process capability, statistical process control (SPC), six sigma, and total quality management (TQM). Improvement: failure mode effect analysis (FMEA), Pareto analysis, cause and effect diagrams, and quality circles. Students need to know the function/purpose of standards and how to access them, the roles of the engineering bodies, the difference between quality control and quality assurance, the main requirements of quality standards, why document/version control matters, when SPC beats 100% sampling, six sigma for high volume manufacture, and the trade offs of different quality improvement approaches. 11.2 Types and applications of Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) and their purposes Covers SOP types and applications (manufacturing, quality, maintenance) and purposes (standardising activity, customer satisfaction, safety, training). Students need to know the typical format/content of an SOP, how they're used in different applications, why they're used (consistency, conformance to standards), and how they're produced, implemented and evaluated. Lesson slides for this section: Quality Management and SOPs (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 12. Health and safety principles and coverage 12.1 The main requirements of key health and safety legislation applicable to engineering activities Key UK legislation students must know the main requirements of, and how it affects their own workplace activities: the Health and Safety at Work Act (HASAWA), Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations, PUWER, PPE Regulations, the Control of Noise at Work Regulations, Manual Handling Operations Regulations, LOLER, Work at Height Regulations, Electricity at Work Regulations, CEMFAW, RIDDOR, and COSHH. Learners don't need to know every legal detail, since company safe systems of work and procedures should already satisfy the legislation but they should understand why the legislation exists, that it covers every aspect of the workplace, how it keeps them safe, who's responsible for compliance, and the role of safety culture, training and information. 12.2 The importance of health and safety practices within the workplace Covers how legislation affects accident/incident frequency, the importance of mental health and wellbeing at work, who's responsible for compliance (employer, employee, the Health and Safety Executive/HSE), and the implications of non compliance. 12.3 Responsibilities for health and safety Employee responsibilities include working safely, not attempting untrained/unauthorised tasks, co operating with the employer, respecting duties placed on the employer or others, and not interfering with or misusing safety provisions. Employer responsibilities include minimising handling/storage/transport risks, providing instruction/training/supervision, maintaining a safe workplace, providing a health and safety policy statement, arranging safety representatives/committees, and protecting visitors, contractors and the public. Students should also know the differences between local, national and global requirements. Lesson slides for this section: Health and Safety Legislation and Responsibilities (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 12.4 Risk assessment Covers the stages of risk assessment: identifying hazards (HAZOP, HAZID), evaluating risk (likelihood, severity, number of people affected), and implementing control measures using the hierarchy of control (elimination, reduction/substitution, isolation, engineering controls, administration/training/safe systems of work, PPE). Students need to know engineering hazards (equipment, stored energy, tools, electricity, harmful substances/gases, environments), common industrial injuries, hazard identification methods, how to evaluate risk, the hierarchy of control, and typical control measures (guarding, machine isolation, PPE such as eye/ear protection, safety shoes, gauntlets, helmets). 12.5 Health and safety considerations in specific engineering contexts Covers considerations (safe systems of work, oxygen use, asphyxiation hazards, heat, moving parts, fire/explosion hazards, fire safety, guarding, manual handling, permit to work, lock out tag out/LOTO, maintenance) across contexts including chemicals, equipment with moving parts, confined spaces, electrical testing, and high voltage electrical work (generation, distribution, isolation, storage). Lesson slides for this section: Risk Assessment and Hazardous Contexts (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 12.6 Principles and practices relating to environmental legislation and considerations Key legislation: the Environmental Protection Act, Pollution Prevention and Control Act, Clean Air Act, Radioactive Substances Act, Controlled Waste Regulations, Dangerous Substances legislation, and Hazardous Waste Regulations. Considerations: ISO 14001 and waste disposal. Students need to know the main requirements and purpose of this legislation, who's responsible for compliance, the aims/benefits/consequences of ISO 14001, and waste disposal methods (landfill, reuse, recycling, controlled waste) and their implications. Lesson slides for this section: Environmental Legislation and Waste (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 13. Business, commercial and financial awareness 13.1 Principles of commercial operations and markets Covers commercial priorities (profit, stakeholder needs), efficiency, value added versus non value added activity, competition, supply and demand, and markets (local, national, international customers). Students need to know the goals of commercial operations, how organisations address different customer/market needs, how activities are evaluated on quality/cost/time, and the role of R&D and innovation. 13.2 Business and commercial practices Covers legal practices (tendering, contracts, warranties, force majeure, indemnity clauses, liabilities), management practices (resource allocation and planning, staffing, training and development), business models (traditional, agile), and company management systems/policies/procedures. Students need to know how these practices influence engineering organisations and the legislation affecting tendering and contracts. 13.3 Financial and economic concepts Covers financial responsibility, recording transactions, sources of finance (loans, shares, capital), budgets, costs (direct, indirect, overheads), payment terms, revenue, creditors/debtors, cash flow, profit and loss, break even, assets (depreciation), liabilities, solvency, taxes and rates. Students need to know what each concept means and its implications for running a business. Lesson slides for this section: Business, Commercial and Financial Awareness (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 14. Professional responsibilities, attitudes, and behaviours 14.1 Professional conduct and responsibilities in the workplace Covers job descriptions, expected workplace behaviours, personal conduct (reputation, ethical responsibility), levels of accountability in organisational structures (apprentice, operator, management, director), and equality/diversity/accessibility/inclusion. Students need to know the purpose of job descriptions, how conduct affects workplace interactions, how to seek advice, expectations around reputation and ethics, the responsibilities of different organisational roles, and an organisation's duties around equality/diversity/accessibility/inclusion. 14.2 Continuous professional development (CPD) and professional recognition Covers CPD routes (training courses, industry placement, academic study, events/seminars). Students need to know what CPD is and how it motivates staff and improves performance, and the professional standards for engineering set by the Engineering Council. 14.3 Human factors within engineering and manufacturing contexts Covers human factors: human characteristics (physical, mental), workplace design considerations, and human error. Students need to know how human characteristics/capabilities/limitations affect a company and its production, how workplace design affects safety/comfort/productivity, and the causes of human error (insufficient training, fatigue, workload, stress) and how to reduce them. Lesson slides for this section: Professional Conduct, CPD and Human Factors (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 15. Stock and asset management 15.1 Stock and inventory management principles and practices Principles: demand, stock turnover, cost of inventory, redundant stock/write down, obsolescence, minimum stock levels, supply chain, packaging/storage. Practices: just in time, made to stock, made to order, material requirements planning. Students need to know the purpose of effective stock/inventory management, and the risks/advantages/disadvantages of each practice. 15.2 Asset management and control principles Covers capacity management (manufacturing resource planning, bottlenecks), the stages of asset life cycle management (planning, acquisition, operation and maintenance, disposal), and budgetary control practices (life cycle/whole life approach, depreciation). Students need to know the purpose and methodology of effective asset management and the trade offs between capacity management methods. Lesson slides for this section: Stock and Asset Management (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 16. Continuous improvement 16.1 Continuous improvement principles and practices Principles: reflection and evaluation of processes, incremental change, key performance indicators (KPIs), the PDCA cycle (plan, do, check, act), the 8 wastes (transportation, inventory, motion, waiting, excess production, overprocessing, defects, unused talent), lean, and Kaizen. Practices: value stream mapping, visual management, 6S (sort, set in order, shine, standardise, sustain, safety), SMED (single minute exchange of dies), OEE (overall equipment effectiveness), TPM (total productive maintenance), and kanban. Students need to know how to gather feedback/evidence about performance (including KPI types) to evaluate improvement activity, how the 8 wastes affect engineering performance, and the purpose/methodology/benefits/limitations of each practice. Lesson slides for this section: Continuous Improvement (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 17. Project and programme management 17.1 Principles of project management Covers the project brief, goals and success criteria, the project life cycle (initiation, planning, implementation, monitoring, reporting, evaluation), constraints and risk management (budget, cost, quality, time, safety, resource availability, communication, reputation, changing requirements), and collaborative working (matrix working, collaborative technologies). Students need to know how projects are structured, the documentation/practices needed at each stage, how risk is managed through a project's life (including the role of R&D), and the benefits/limitations of collaborative working. 17.2 Roles and responsibilities in projects Covers roles (stakeholders including clients and regulators, project manager, team members) and responsibilities (communication, monitoring, planning, finance, reporting). Students need to know how each role contributes to a project. 17.3 Project planning and control Planning: resource requirements (time, budget, people, training, communication, production facilities), Gantt charts, critical path analysis (CPA), PERT, managing interdependencies, contingency planning. Control: monitoring reports (budget, quality, cost, time), managing by stages, managing by exception. Students need to know how to identify resource requirements, the benefits/limitations of different planning methods, how to plan using them, and how to monitor, evaluate and review projects to improve future ones. title: Employer-set Project
text: Employer set Project Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Core Component → Employer set Project The Employer set project (ESP) is one of three assessment components in the core, worth 30% of the core and 18.5 hours of assessment time. It's externally set and externally marked by City & Guilds, and it's designed to make learners identify and use, in an integrated way, an appropriate selection of skills, techniques, concepts, theories and knowledge drawn from across the whole engineering common core content. Lesson slides for this section: The Employer set Project (PowerPoint, 13 slides) What the project involves The ESP consists of a well defined, real industry style brief. The brief is complex and non routine, and requires learners to use relevant maths, English and digital skills to respond to it. It gives learners a valid context to demonstrate their knowledge of the core content and their core skills by solving occupationally relevant situations or problems. Each project is developed together with employers to reflect realistic types of developments, activities and challenges in the sector. The project is made up of several tasks, all relating to the same ESP brief, covering: Research Design Plan Present It draws on knowledge from the core content shared across all four Design and Development specialisms (specialism specific knowledge and skills are instead assessed separately in each specialism's practical assignment for this guide, see Mechanical Engineering: Practical Criteria). The project is also linked to four core skills: planning and preparation, communication, develop and manufacture, and evaluation. How it's delivered Projects are released to centre staff in advance of each assessment window. City & Guilds provides centres with assessment windows in which to timetable assessment sessions, following the timings set out in the ESP centre guidance. Centres must keep all live assessment materials secure until the assessment window opens projects are password protected and released through a secure method. Guidance on equipment, resources and duration is released in advance so centres can plan delivery. Learners who fail the ESP on first submission can retake it in any assessment window, provided the retake is completed within one year of finishing the T Level programme. Assessment objectives AO Focus Weighting AO1 Plan approach to meeting the brief evidence of a planned, sequenced, prioritised and iterative approach; a clearly structured, cohesive response; logical referencing/research/sourcing; meeting the brief's parameters; effective use of presentation time. 13% AO2 Apply core knowledge and skills as appropriate linking knowledge, principles and ideas and applying them in the context of the brief (materials, concepts, etc.), and applying core skills like communication and planning throughout the project's tasks. 50% AO3 Select relevant techniques and resources to meet the brief choosing effective, appropriate techniques and resources, and using them accurately and with understanding. 13% AO4 Use maths, English and digital skills correct terminology/abbreviations/units, considering the audience (technical vs. non technical wording), appropriate use of calculations/diagrams, and appropriate use of ICT/digital methods in both the response and its presentation. 10% AO5 Realise project outcome and review how well the outcome meets the brief analysing and evaluating the outcome, drawing conclusions, identifying solutions to the brief's problem, and evaluating other options considered and why they were rejected. 13% Weightings are rounded to the nearest whole number. title: Core Scheme of Assessment
text: Core Scheme of Assessment Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Core Component → Core Scheme of Assessment The core component is assessed through two externally set, externally marked exams (worth 35% of the core each) and the Employer set Project (worth 30% of the core). The whole core component is graded on the A E scale, plus Ungraded (U). Core exam structure Paper Method Duration Marks Weighting Marking Exam paper 1 Externally set exam 2.5 hours 100 35% Externally marked Exam paper 2 Externally set exam 2.5 hours 100 35% Externally marked Employer set project Externally set project 18.5 hours 90 30% Externally marked The exams are made up of short answer questions (SAQs, some structured) and extended response questions (ERQs), sat under invigilated examination conditions. Question difficulty increases through each paper, from lower demand questions at the start to higher demand questions at the end. Learners who need to retake the core exams must retake both exams in the same assessment window, within one year of completing their T Level programme. What each paper covers Paper 1 draws on: essential mathematics, essential science, materials and their properties, mechanical principles, electrical and electronic principles, and mechatronics. Paper 2 draws on: working within the sector, engineering and manufacturing past/present/future, engineering representations, control systems, quality management, health and safety, business/commercial/financial awareness, professional responsibilities/attitudes/behaviours, stock and asset management, continuous improvement, and project and programme management. Assessment objectives (core exams) AO Description Weighting AO1a Demonstrate knowledge Basic recall of relevant knowledge in response to straightforward questions, e.g. material properties. 10% AO1b Demonstrate understanding Explaining principles and concepts beyond recall of definitions, in a general way outside a particular context, e.g. simple engineering terms and concepts. 22% AO2 Apply knowledge and understanding to different situations and context Applying understanding of generalities to specific situations, e.g. applying a single concept or an essential mathematical concept to a straightforward situation. 46% AO3 Analyse and evaluate information and issues Analysing the interrelated issues in a complex scenario and evaluating them to propose a best solution or predict impacts, e.g. evaluating material properties and requirements for an engineered product. 22% All three AOs require the ability to recall knowledge, but they build on each other: AO1 covers basic recall plus explaining/summarising concepts in the learner's own words; AO2 is about applying that understanding to specific, concrete (if fairly granular) situations; AO3 is the most demanding, requiring analysis and evaluation of a detailed or complex scenario, problem or data set, with marks awarded for the quality and range of the analysis. For the Employer set Project's own assessment objectives (AO1 AO5, different from the core exam AOs above), see Employer set Project. Key terms SAQ / ERQ short answer question / extended response question, the two main question formats in the core exams. AO Assessment Objective, a weighted criterion markers use to grade a piece of assessed work. Ungraded (U) the below a pass outcome on the core component's A E grading scale. title: Occupational Specialism Overview
text: Occupational Specialism Overview Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Occupational Specialism → Overview This T Level offers four occupational specialism pathways nationally: Mechanical Engineering, Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Control and Instrumentation Engineering, and Structural Engineering. This study guide covers Mechanical Engineering only , as that's the pathway taught at UTC Leeds the other three are not included here. Designing, developing and testing mechanical solutions. What this specialism is about The Mechanical Engineering specialism is worth 680 Guided Learning Hours and is assessed by a practical assignment. Its purpose is for learners to know and undertake designing and development processes within mechanical engineering planning, performing and evaluating their own work using a range of techniques, methods and resources. Learners develop knowledge and skills in: design methodologies and processes the tools, equipment and materials used in mechanical engineering mathematical theories and methods used in mechanical engineering producing mechanical drawings and representations designing and developing working models testing models and prototypes Learners might approach the specialism by asking themselves questions such as: what different types of mechanical systems are there and what are they used for? What do mechanical engineers do on a daily basis? What areas of the engineering industry do mechanical engineers work in? Underpinning knowledge and Performance Outcomes On completion of the specialism, learners understand: 1. Mechanical engineering knowledge criteria see Knowledge Criteria. And are able to (the five Performance Outcomes, all covered together in Practical Criteria): 2. Analyse and interpret engineering and manufacturing requirements, systems, processes, technical drawings and specifications. 3. Evaluate systems, designs, components and processes, managing and integrating design information, proposals and specifications, to develop and improve mechanical engineering and manufacturing proposals and solutions. 4. Propose and design mechanical engineering and manufacturing systems, products, components, processes and solutions, considering requirements, constraints and context. 5. Collaborate to help manage, develop, test and quality assure mechanical engineering and manufacturing design information, systems, processes and outcomes. 6. Communicate proposals, design information and solutions, producing, recording and explaining engineering and manufacturing representations, systems, processes, outcomes, specifications and technical drawings. Completing the specialism also gives learners the chance to develop their maths, English and digital skills see Competency Frameworks. How it's assessed The specialism is assessed by one practical assignment , lasting 33 hours 40 minutes, made up of four tasks (design, manufacture and test, peer review, evaluation and implementation). See Scheme of Assessment for the full breakdown. Key terms Performance Outcome (PO) one of the 5 numbered practical/skills outcomes (PO2 PO6) learners are assessed against. Outcome 1 the underpinning knowledge outcome ("Mechanical engineering knowledge criteria"), assessed through how it's applied across the practical assignment rather than as a separate written test. Range the source specification's term for the specific scope (materials, methods, standards, etc.) a subtopic covers. title: Knowledge Criteria
text: Knowledge Criteria Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Occupational Specialism → Knowledge Criteria This page covers Outcome 1: Common knowledge criteria for the Mechanical Engineering specialism the underpinning knowledge that supports all five Performance Outcomes (analysing requirements, evaluating designs, proposing solutions, collaborating, and communicating see Practical Criteria). Subsection numbers (1.1, 1.2...) mirror the specification. 1.1 Principles of engineering design Covers requirements (functionality, aesthetics, dimensions, ergonomics, safety, sustainability, cost, materials), how requirements are identified (market research, client interviews/observation, product analysis) and recorded (design briefs, specifications, questionnaires, observational records), factors that affect design (product life cycle, sustainability, safety), the fields within mechanical engineering (design; manufacture and processing; fitting and assembly maintenance), and ways of communicating designs (orthographic drawings, virtual models, physical models). Learners need to know how to agree the scope of a project, identify/confirm/record client requirements accurately, evaluate and develop those requirements, and communicate design ideas and technical information clearly including the tools available for recording and developing requirements. 1.2 Design methodologies Covers the systems approach, sub assembly, and component by component methodologies. Learners need to understand design practices including planned obsolescence, the contexts different methodologies suit, their purpose/benefits/limitations, how to interpret anthropometric data tables for ergonomic design, and how process capability and tolerances influence Design for Manufacture/Assembly (DFM/DFA). Lesson slides for this section: Design Principles, Methodologies and Verification (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 1.3 Engineering representations Covers the characteristics of orthographic drawings (sheet size, section views/hatching), and the information conveyed by drawings (standard features like springs, splines, gears, webs, solid shafts, keys/keyways; mechanical symbols like balloon, diameter, depth). Learners need to know the purpose and audience of different drawing types, and how to interpret the symbols, conventions and annotations used in BS EN 8888. 1.4 Standards and regulatory requirements Covers relevant bodies British Standards (BSI), International Organization for Standardization (ISO), Institution of Mechanical Engineers (IMechE). Learners need to know the purpose and requirements of these standards for mechanical component design, their key responsibilities and codes, and how to access and interpret regulatory requirements and responsibilities. Lesson slides for this section: Mechanical Drawings, Standards and Communication (PowerPoint, 14 slides) 1.5 Mathematical theories and methods Covers gear ratio, velocity ratio, mechanical advantage, efficiency, stress, strain, pressure, density, velocity and acceleration. Learners need to be able to calculate these in relation to resource requirements, material properties, mechanical system characteristics and drawing representations, and apply the underlying theories in context. 1.6 Simple machines Covers gears, pulleys, levers, linkages, cams and ratchets. Learners need to know how each type changes the magnitude, direction or type of motion; the types and applications of gears (spur, helical, bevel, worm, rack and pinion) including calculations for simple and compound gear trains; types and applications of levers (class 1, 2, 3); types and applications of linkages (reverse motion, parallel motion, bell crank, crank and slider); and types and applications of cams (circular, eccentric, snail). Lesson slides for this section: Simple Machines and Mechanical Calculations (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 1.7 Influence of engineering requirements on design outcomes Covers mechanical loads (static/dynamic/structural/fluid loading, point loading, uniform loading, torque, shear forces, bending moments, fatigue) and service/environmental conditions (chemical attack/corrosion, temperature, functional properties). Learners need to know how load type affects mechanical properties, how environmental conditions affect material characteristics and functionality, and other factors (manufacturing, material choice) that shape a design outcome. Lesson slides for this section: Loads, Environment and Aerodynamics in Design (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 1.8 Verification and validation in design practices Covers comparing outcomes against the brief/specification, user testing, comparison matrices, ranking, decision trees and functional testing. Learners need to know the difference between verification and validation, where each applies, why meeting specifications matters at each design stage, the relative advantages/limitations of each approach, and how these methods confirm an outcome meets its original specification. Lesson slides for this section: Design Principles, Methodologies and Verification (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 1.9 Business context, constraints and metrics Covers context (market pull vs. technology push, commercial advantage, design for reuse, planned obsolescence, sustainability); constraints (commercial factors like competition/profitability, operational factors like tools/equipment/materials/process capability/human resources/training/legal/confidentiality, design for manufacture); and metrics (budget, cost, profit, time). Learners need to understand market pull vs. technology push, how context influences product design, how to calculate manufacturing cost (materials, labour, overheads) and profit, why constraints exist and how they can be overcome, and the impact of commercial risk analysis on project design review. Lesson slides for this section: Business Context, Constraints and Metrics in Design (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 1.10 Materials and standard parts Covers considerations (fitness for purpose, material availability, managing risk, factor of safety) and material families: ferrous metals (cast iron, low/medium/high carbon steel, stainless steel), non ferrous metals (aluminium and alloys, copper, brass and bronze, nickel, zinc), thermoplastic polymers (ABS, HIPS, PLA, polycarbonate, polypropylene, PMMA/acrylic), thermosetting polymers (urea formaldehyde, melamine formaldehyde, phenol formaldehyde, epoxy resin, polyester resin), elastomers (rubber, neoprene), composites (GRP, CRP), engineering ceramics (silicon carbide, glass), and smart materials (shape memory alloys, quantum tunnelling composite, thermochromic/photochromic materials, piezoelectric crystals). Also covers standard parts (valves, sensors, piping, supports and fittings) and why companies use them instead of manufacturing their own. 1.11 Influence of manufacturing processes on design Covers wasting processes (cutting, filing, turning, milling, grinding), shaping (casting, moulding), forming (bending, pressing), welding (MIG/MAG, TIG), 3D printing, joining, finishing and assembly. Learners need to know how each process forms products, the tools/equipment typically used, comparative advantages and disadvantages, and why tolerances and fits matter for assembly. Lesson slides for this section: Materials, Standard Parts and Manufacturing Processes (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 1.12 Aerodynamic forces on design Covers fluid flow (laminar flow, separation points, vortices, turbulence), lift, drag, turbulence and thrust. Learners need to be able to interpret 2D representations of fluid flow around simple objects, and understand how lift, drag, thrust and turbulence apply aerodynamic loading to structures. Lesson slides for this section: Loads, Environment and Aerodynamics in Design (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 1.13 Mathematical calculations for design development Covers force calculations (stress, strain, Young's modulus, structural member loading compressive/tensile and beam analysis for simply supported/cantilever beams including reactions, shear force and bending moment); material requirement calculations (quantity by area/volume/units, material and manufacturing cost); and machine performance calculations (load, effort, mechanical advantage, velocity ratio, work, energy, power, efficiency). Lesson slides for this section: Simple Machines and Mechanical Calculations (PowerPoint, 16 slides) 1.14 Health and safety in mechanical engineering Covers the Environmental Protection Act, Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations (LOLER), Manual Handling Operations Regulations, and PUWER. Learners need to know the specific procedures, protocols and legal/regulatory requirements that apply to mechanical engineering design and development activity, the importance of and route to compliance, and employer/employee responsibilities under the regulations. Lesson slides for this section: Health and Safety Legislation and Responsibilities (PowerPoint, 13 slides) 1.15 Quality factors, assurance and control Covers assignable/systematic error causes (faulty equipment calibration, tool wear, observer bias, human error) versus random causes (ambient/environmental conditions, temperature, humidity, instrument uncertainty); and quality control practices quality assurance (procedures, calibration, process capability monitoring, preventative maintenance) versus quality control (testing, inspection). Learners need to know the difference between assignable and random causes, how each results in errors and how that risk can be reduced, why process checks/inspections are necessary, the trade off between sampling and 100% inspection, and how production quantity shapes the quality approach. Lesson slides for this section: Quality, Testing and Measurement (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 1.16 Installation and integration of systems Covers installation (customer requirements, regulatory requirements, manufacturer specifications) and integration (combining systems, functions, designs, planning, processes). Learners need to know the requirements/procedures/considerations for installing mechanical systems, the key stages and sequence of system integration, and how sub systems are brought together into one functioning system. Lesson slides for this section: Installation and Integration of Systems (PowerPoint, 12 slides) 1.17 Testing methods Covers non destructive testing (visual inspection, measurement, Go/No Go gauges, ultrasonic testing, penetrant testing, magnetic particle inspection, X radiography) and destructive testing (macro examination, hardness testing, tensile testing, impact tests such as Izod and Charpy). Learners need to know each method's methodology, the types of defect each detects, and the relative benefits/limitations of each. 1.18 Measurement equipment Covers rules, protractors, callipers (Vernier, digital), micrometres (outside, inside, depth), gauges (go/no go, slip, plug), dial test indicators, coordinate measuring machines (CMMs), laser scanning, and digital stress/strain machines. Learners need to know what each item measures and how it's used, its accuracy and relative limitations/benefits, and technology used to measure other mechanical characteristics such as air flow. 1.19 Mathematical methods for measurement and performance data Covers processing test results and performance data. Learners need to be able to determine and analyse statistical values when measuring, checking and confirming test and performance data. Lesson slides for this section: Quality, Testing and Measurement (PowerPoint, 15 slides) 1.20 Communicating mechanical engineering information Covers methods (CAD models, engineering drawings, written data such as specifications/SOPs/reports, presentations, transmitting instructions to CNC machines via direct entry/intranet/WiFi, graphs of performance data/test results/SPC) and audiences (designers, manufacturing engineers, customers, non technical personnel). Learners need to know the media/formats/conventions used to communicate engineering data (including BS 8888), how to transfer data from CAD to CAM, the applications and benefits of 2D versus 3D CAD, how CAE tools visualise simulated CAD assembly performance, and the uses of visualisation software.
