title: Practical Criteria
text: Practical Criteria Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Occupational Specialism → Practical Criteria This page covers the Practical criteria for Performance Outcomes 2 6 the hands on skills side of the Mechanical Engineering specialism, sitting alongside the underpinning Knowledge Criteria. Subsection numbers (2.1, 3.1...) mirror the specification. Outcome 2: Analyse and interpret engineering and manufacturing requirements, systems, processes, technical drawings and specifications 2.1 Access, interpret and respond to design projects and tasks. Learners access, examine, interpret, review and respond to information from sources such as design briefs, specifications, concept drawings and stakeholders (supervisors, colleagues, clients/end users). 2.2 Evaluate project expectations and requirements, including risk. Learners determine and evaluate materials requirements, manufacturing timescale and cost for a specified project, and identify risks (design and/or commercial) to a project along with mitigation actions. 2.3 Interpret, evaluate and modify engineering information. Covers a range of formats: specifications, CAD models, engineering drawings, mechanical process and instrument diagrams, standard operating procedures, production plans. Learners interpret information from these sources, identify inaccuracies/errors and how to correct them, and identify and manage scope creep or process driven design change, escalating or reporting as necessary. 2.4 Verify mechanical design information against context, function and requirements. Covers information sources (concept drawings, briefs, specifications) and requirements (components, materials, application, location, risk, environment). Learners interpret design information and evaluate whether a proposal actually meets the requirements. 2.5 Use technology to evaluate mechanical design elements. Covers technology (mathematical calculations, CAD simulations, physical modelling) applied to design elements (systems, components, assemblies, products, processes). Learners use appropriate technology, including CAD, to review, analyse and interpret design elements in proposals and products. Lesson slides for this section: Analysing Requirements and Design Information (PowerPoint, 13 slides) Outcome 3: Evaluate systems, designs, components and processes, managing and integrating design information, proposals and specifications, to develop and improve mechanical engineering and manufacturing proposals and solutions 3.1 Select and use technology to model and evaluate design performance. Covers mathematical modelling tools, spreadsheets, and CAD simulations, evaluated against features, issues and current/potential performance. Learners weigh cost, availability, compatibility, training needs and time when selecting a tool, and choose the tool most relevant to the failure modes being assessed. 3.2 Analyse factors affecting mechanical designs and justify recommendations. Covers materials, application, location, risk, environment, configuration, geometry and scale. Learners assess and prioritise these factors, compare which apply generally versus only in certain situations, and understand the difference between optimising an existing design and developing a new one. 3.3 Select and justify materials for specific uses. Covers the same material families as the knowledge criteria (ferrous/non ferrous metals, thermoplastics, thermosets, elastomers, composites, engineering ceramics, smart materials). Learners use appropriate information sources on material properties and justify a material choice with reference to context. 3.4 Apply knowledge of material degradation and failure to evaluate proposals. Covers chemical attack/corrosion, fracture, mechanical abrasion, creep and fatigue. Learners apply this knowledge, plus prevention/mitigation methods, to investigate and evaluate design proposals, processes and outcomes. 3.5 Review and confirm the relevance, implications and value of test results. Covers the same non destructive and destructive testing methods as the knowledge criteria. Learners determine a test's relevance and value, use results to influence the design, and consider the purpose, context, traceability, recording and reporting of tests, modelling and research. 3.6 Evaluate designs and design processes against application requirements. Covers quality and performance evaluation against purpose/functionality, environmental/working conditions, and application requirements like cost and value engineering. Learners assess the fitness for purpose of both the design and the process used to reach it. 3.7 Compare alternative design options and identify improvements. Learners compare and evaluate design options, iterations and processes to determine the best solution, using criteria such as fitness for purpose, context, constraints, agreed metrics and specification compliance. 3.8 Review individual, team and organisational performance across the design and manufacture process. Covers design methods, quality systems, standards, manufacturing methods, performance targets and KPIs. Learners reflect on and identify potential improvements. 3.9 Respond constructively and creatively to project/task changes and feedback. Learners follow a process for confirming the scope of new requirements and the route to revising or resolving them, understand the importance of responding constructively, and log/record changes throughout the design process. Lesson slides for this section: Evaluating and Improving Designs (PowerPoint, 13 slides) Outcome 4: Propose and design mechanical engineering and manufacturing systems, products, components, processes and solutions, considering requirements, constraints and context 4.1 Propose and develop designs to address requirements. Covers requirements from the design brief, specification, mechanical principles (scientific, mathematical) and material properties. Learners take ideas and sketch them into detailed concepts, annotating to show where requirements are addressed and justifying material choices. 4.2 Practically model and calculate mechanical system performance. Covers linear systems (levers, linkages), rotating systems (gears, flywheels) and lifting machines (cranes, pulleys). Learners model and calculate dynamic effects from acceleration, determine rotating system performance, and analyse lifting machine characteristics and operation. 4.3 Produce effective representations using CAD software, tools and technology. Covers sketching (freehand and isometric), 2D and 3D drawings, models, simulations and accurate 3D assemblies, using 3D CAD solid modelling and manual techniques. Learners use tools safely and effectively, access support when needed, and judge which representation type suits a given situation (e.g. model versus 2D drawing). 4.4 Produce detailed engineering drawings to relevant standards and codes. Covers British Standards, ISO standards, CE marking and engineering bodies (Engineering Council, IET, IMechE, SOE). Learners follow a process to produce accurate, detailed drawings, considering accuracy, tolerances, units, scale and correct symbols. 4.5 Develop high quality working models meeting functional and non functional requirements. Covers block models, rapid prototyped/3D printed models and one off prototype manufacture, against requirements like dimensions (fit, form), aesthetics, mechanical properties and cost. Learners apply design, manufacturing and production principles, following safe working practices. 4.6 Use basic hand and powered tools safely to carry out basic engineering processes. Covers common hand/power tools (screwdriver, hacksaw, hammer, files, Allen keys, spanner, socket set, wrench, glue gun, drill, pliers, rule, set square, protractor, Vernier callipers, micrometres) and processes (wasting, shaping, forming, welding, 3D printing). Learners select and use appropriate tools, carry out pre/during/post use safety checks (calibration, storage, reporting damage), and must use at least one welding type and one 3D printing type when prototyping. 4.7 Assemble and disassemble mechanical systems. Covers assembly (configuration, sequencing, aligning, bending, fixing, mechanical jointing, pre tensioning, sealing, sequential tightening, threaded jointing/locking devices, functional testing) and disassembly (releasing tension/pressure, proof marking, safe tool use). Learners work safely and follow established protocols, including ensuring appropriate training has been given. 4.8 Produce high quality designs of realisable mechanical systems that satisfy requirements. Covers standards, functional requirements (dimensions, mechanical properties, aesthetics, maintenance) and non functional requirements (cost, quality). Learners test and evaluate finished products, demonstrate commercial realisability, and check designs can actually be manufactured, operated and maintained. Lesson slides for this section: Designing, Modelling and Prototyping (PowerPoint, 13 slides) Outcome 5: Collaborate to help manage, develop, test and quality assure mechanical engineering and manufacturing design information, systems, processes and outcomes 5.1 Follow professional standards, management systems, policies and safe working practice. Covers professional standards (Engineering Council, IMechE, IET) and policies/procedures (workplace policies, SOPs, national/industry health and safety requirements). Learners identify where standards/policies sit, understand the consequences of not following them, and assess/manage/mitigate risk in mechanical engineering contexts. 5.2 Work effectively with others to agree and complete tasks. Covers tasks such as design, development, investigation, research, problem solving, testing, validation, quality assurance/control, and producing/interpreting documentation. Learners contribute effectively, respond to others' input, and understand how timeframes, deadlines and dynamic conditions affect a task. 5.3 Complete detailed risk management analyses in response to project requirements. Learners carry out risk management and identify mitigation actions in contexts like machining, mechanical handling and high power applications, respond appropriately to unfamiliar situations, and understand commercial risk ranking models. 5.4 Develop and test models and prototypes of design proposals. Covers virtual and physical models (block, rapid prototyped/3D printed, one off prototype manufacture). Learners produce models using different methodologies, test/assess/report/respond to model performance, and carry out concept testing, functional tests, measurements and visual inspection of production prototypes. 5.5 Produce and quality assure design information to professional standards. Covers design information (proposals, specifications, engineering drawings, technical information) against professional standards (Engineering Council, IMechE, IET). Learners produce, manage, quality assure and validate this information, and check completed drawings for quality, technical compliance and completeness. Lesson slides for this section: Collaboration, Risk and Quality Assurance (PowerPoint, 13 slides) Outcome 6: Communicate proposals, design information and solutions, producing, recording and explaining engineering and manufacturing representations, systems, processes, outcomes, specifications and technical drawings 6.1 Produce and manage technical documentation using digital tools and conventions. Covers technical documentation (design specifications, engineering drawings) and digital tools (CAD software, document management systems, SharePoint, spreadsheets). Learners produce, amend, check, manage and version control documentation using appropriate conventions and protocols, use collaborative digital tools to manage and quality assure information, and annotate drawings (geometrical tolerances, limits and fits, surface finishes). 6.2 Communicate design information and options with technical and non technical audiences. Covers design information (specifications, proposals, working drawings, representations, technical/non technical data, systems, processes, risks, outcomes), audiences (stakeholders, colleagues, clients) and formats (sketches, schemes, detailed drawings, diagrams, models, reports). Learners select formats suited to cost, time, availability, end user and project scale, clearly evidence stages of the design process, and communicate/coordinate design information across audiences. Lesson slides for this section: Technical Documentation and Communication (PowerPoint, 12 slides) Guidance for delivery Providers are encouraged to arrange visits to and engagement with local industry, employers and manufacturers throughout delivery local employers presenting recent projects (including problems faced and how they were solved) is suggested, as is learners presenting their own work placement experiences to peers. Formative assessment can include oral Q&A, peer presentations, and observation of measuring activities; learning can be reinforced through revisiting content, group discussion and peer support within the cohort. Providers must keep delivery aligned with current industry practice providing appropriate tools, equipment and test instrumentation, and teaching on equipment representative of what's actually used in UK industry. Suggested resources include Marks' Standard Handbook for Mechanical Engineers (Avallone, Baumeister & Sadeh), Machinery's Handbook (McCauley), and Engineering Project Management (Smith), alongside the Institution of Mechanical Engineers (imeche.org) and Health and Safety Executive (hse.gov.uk) websites. title: Scheme of Assessment
text: Scheme of Assessment Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Occupational Specialism → Scheme of Assessment This page covers how the Mechanical Engineering specialism is assessed: the practical assignment's structure, its four tasks, and how each Performance Outcome is weighted. Structure The specialism is assessed by one practical assignment , lasting 33 hours 40 minutes . Learners are assessed against four assessment themes running through the tasks: Health and safety Design and planning Manufacturing Reports The four tasks Task 1 Design. Learners plan and design a prototype/model, producing documents and drawings to industry standards showing how they'll develop it in line with the brief, using CAD software to produce engineering drawings and a virtual model. Learners also give feedback on a peer's engineering drawings. Task 2 Manufacture and test. Learners manufacture and test the prototype/model in line with their planning and designs, working in a clear, logical sequence, safely, and interpreting/recording test results accurately, selecting and using tools/materials/equipment correctly. Task 3 Peer review. Learners discuss designs with peers to gain feedback that informs adaptations to their own design before implementation, and give constructive critique with recommendations on others' designs. Task 4 Evaluation and implementation. Learners evaluate their own design and manufacture, recommending adaptations and improvements, justifying their test methods, providing enough information for a third party to implement the model, and justifying how peer feedback was considered and implemented. Performance Outcome weighting Each Performance Outcome is drawn on by specific tasks and evidenced through specific outputs: Performance Outcome Weighting Tasks it draws on Typical evidence PO2 Analyse and interpret requirements/systems/processes/drawings/specifications 16% T1, T2, T4 Design specification, annotated sketches, virtual modelling, design calculations; manufacture of the prototype; evaluation and implementation report PO3 Evaluate systems/designs/components/processes to develop and improve solutions 22% T1, T2, T4 Engineering drawings, virtual modelling, bill of materials; manufacture of the prototype; evaluation report, revision control document PO4 Propose and design systems/products/components/processes/solutions 23% T1, T2 Design specification, sketches, engineering drawings, virtual modelling; manufacture and testing of the prototype, records of testing PO5 Collaborate to manage/develop/test/quality assure 26% T2, T4 Manufacture and testing of the prototype, risk assessment; evaluation report, records of testing, revision control document PO6 Communicate proposals/design information/solutions 13% T1, T4 Engineering drawings, design specification, annotated sketches, records of testing, virtual modelling; evaluation and implementation report Every task also maps onto one or more of the four assessment themes (health and safety, design and planning, manufacturing, reports) for example, Task 1 evidence is assessed under "design and planning" and "health and safety", while Task 2 evidence sits under "manufacturing" (and often "health and safety" too). Delivery resources Providers are expected to give learners access to appropriate tools, equipment and test instrumentation that reflects current UK industry practice not just what's convenient to teach with. Suggested textbooks include Marks' Standard Handbook for Mechanical Engineers , Machinery's Handbook , and Engineering Project Management , alongside the Institution of Mechanical Engineers and Health and Safety Executive websites for further reference. Visits to and engagement with local employers/manufacturers are encouraged throughout delivery, not just as one off events. Key terms Assessment theme one of the four cross cutting areas (health and safety, design and planning, manufacturing, reports) that tasks are assessed against. Revision control document a record tracking changes made to a design over the course of a project. title: Competency Frameworks
text: Competency Frameworks Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Appendices Alongside the technical content, this qualification maps a set of core skills , plus general English , maths and digital competencies, onto the core and specialism content. These aren't taught as separate lessons they're signposted against the relevant criteria throughout the specification, wherever there's a natural opportunity to develop them, and each specialism page in this guide notes where a skill applies. The four core skills These four core skills are fundamental to the knowledge, skills and behaviours learners need as they progress beyond the T Level. They've been mapped onto the qualification content in consultation with industry and providers not every piece of content develops a core skill, but where one does, it's referenced. Core Skill A Planning and preparation (DD CSA). Interpreting and confirming project requirements; planning and scoping project parameters (timescales, resources, costs); developing project plans. In practice: preparing a programme and critical path (e.g. in Microsoft Project), a stock inventory plan, a project organigram defining stakeholder roles, sharing documentation via SharePoint, running a commercial risk review, preparing initial costings/budgets, and working collaboratively and ethically with clients, teams and end users. Core Skill B Communication (DD CSB). Interpreting, using and producing engineering representations and drawings to graphical language and industry conventions; interpreting and using technical information and media; communicating with technical and non technical audiences using technology. In practice: sketch designs and 3D models (e.g. SketchUp), AutoCAD drawings for a CNC router, fully dimensioned isometric drawings (e.g. Solidworks), tender documentation, budget spreadsheets, presentations of material options, and reporting dangerous situations during manufacture. Core Skill C Developing proposals and concepts (DD CSC). Designing proposals to meet set requirements; developing, modelling and revising concepts. In practice: complying with a client's brief, producing risk assessments/method statements/safe systems of work, applying lean manufacturing to minimise waste, developing and re evaluating prototypes, planning for production, assessing ergonomics/materials/modularity/sustainability, applying manufacturing standards safely, and considering environmental obligations. Core Skill D Evaluation (DD CSD). Carrying out tests, evaluation and analysis; evaluating how well project requirements have been met. In practice: benchmarking and KPIs, applying manufacturing test methods, using prototypes to evaluate a product against its brief, end of line inspection, the product realisation process, Six Sigma continuous improvement, and testing against current UK/international standards. General English Competencies A framework of six competencies, with no priority order intended: Code Competency EC1 Convey technical information to different audiences EC2 Present information and ideas EC3 Create texts for different purposes and audiences EC4 Summarise information/ideas EC5 Synthesise information EC6 Take part in/lead discussions General Mathematical Competencies A framework of ten competencies, with no priority order intended: Code Competency MC1 Measuring with precision MC2 Estimating, calculating and error spotting MC3 Working with proportion MC4 Using rules and formulae MC5 Processing data MC6 Understanding data and risk MC7 Interpreting and representing with mathematical diagrams MC8 Communicating using mathematics MC9 Costing a project MC10 Optimising work processes General Digital Competencies A framework of six competencies, with no priority order intended: Code Competency DC1 Use digital technology and media effectively DC2 Design, create and edit documents and digital media DC3 Communicate and collaborate DC4 Process and analyse numerical data DC5 Be safe and responsible online DC6 Controlling digital functions Key terms Core skill one of four cross cutting skills (Planning and preparation, Communication, Developing proposals and concepts, Evaluation) mapped across the qualification's content. Signposting the practice of flagging which specific content areas offer a natural opportunity to develop a given English, maths, digital or core skill. title: Help: Using This Wiki
text: Help: Using This Wiki Design and Development for Engineering and Manufacturing T Level → Help This page explains how to get around the site how search works, how the sidebar and breadcrumbs work, and how the wiki relates to the file library in the GitHub repository. Searching Use the search box at the top of every page. It searches the title and full text of every page as you type, not just headings so searching for a specific term (e.g. "tolerancing", "orthographic", "quality management") will surface any page that mentions it, even if it's not in the title. Matching words are highlighted in the results, and each result shows a short snippet of surrounding text plus its file path so you know exactly where it lives. The sidebar directory tree The panel on the left mirrors the content/ folder in the GitHub repository exactly same folders, same files, same order. Click a folder name to expand or collapse it; click a page name to open it. Whatever page you're currently reading is highlighted in the tree, and its parent folders are automatically expanded. On narrow/mobile screens, tap the & 9776; button in the top left to show or hide the sidebar. The breadcrumb and "Contents" box Above every article title is a breadcrumb showing the folder path to that page click any segment to jump to that folder. Longer articles also get an automatically generated Contents box under the introduction, listing every section on the page as a jump link. Categories At the bottom of each article you'll see a Categories line this shows which part of the qualification the page belongs to (e.g. Core Component, or the Occupational Specialism), and clicking a category takes you to that section's overview page. Files vs. website Everything on this site is generated directly from the markdown files in the repository's content/ folder, so the two are always in sync. If you'd rather read the raw files for example, to search across everything at once with your own tools, or to download the whole library you can browse content/ directly on GitHub instead. See the main README for a guided starting point. This isn't the official specification This wiki is an independent, unofficial study guide. It paraphrases and reorganises the real T Level specification to make revision easier, but it is not the exam board's own document, and it can contain mistakes or fall out of date. For anything that actually matters for your assessment, always check the official specification and your course provider. See Sources and Further Reading for more official links. Only one pathway covered This qualification has four occupational specialism pathways (Mechanical Engineering, Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Control and Instrumentation Engineering, Structural Engineering). This wiki covers Mechanical Engineering only , since that's the pathway taught at UTC Leeds.
